ℙ{Rn+1>𝖰1−α(∑j=1n+1w~j⋅δRj)}=?ℙ{Ri>𝖰1−α(∑j=1n+1w~j⋅δRj)}.\mathbb{P}\left\{{R_{n+1}>\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{j}\cdot\delta_{R_{j}}\right)}\right\}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\normalsize?}}}{{=}}\mathbb{P}\left\{{R_{i}>\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{j}\cdot\delta_{R_{j}}\right)}\right\}.

Even when the residuals RiR_{i} are exchangeable (i.e., when the data points are exchangeable and the algorithm is symmetric), the weighted quantile 𝖰1−α​(∑j=1n+1w~j⋅δRj)\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{j}\cdot\delta_{R_{j}}) is no longer a symmetric function of R1,…,Rn+1R_{1},\dots,R_{n+1} if the weights w~j\tilde{w}_{j} are not all equal, and therefore, the equality will no longer be true in general.

Next, if we use nonsymmetric algorithms that take tagged data points (Xi,Yi,ti)(X_{i},Y_{i},t_{i}) as input, the situation becomes even more complex—even if the data points (Xi,Yi)(X_{i},Y_{i}) are exchangeable, the residuals R1,…,Rn+1R_{1},\dots,R_{n+1} may no longer be exchangeable as they depend on a fitted model μ^\widehat{\mu} that treats the training data points nonsymmetrically.

Finally, in this paper we are of course primarily interested in the setting where the data points are no longer exchangeable, and in bounding the resulting coverage gap. This leads to additional challenges, all of which we address in the proofs below.

6.2 Proof of Theorem 2

Since nonexchangeable split conformal is simply a special case of nonexchangeable full conformal, we only need to prove the result for full conformal.

For each k∈[n+1]k\in[n+1], denote

7 Discussion

Our main contribution in this paper was to demonstrate how conformal prediction, which has crucially relied on exchangeability, can be modified to handle nonsymmetric regression algorithms, and utilize weighted residual distributions in order to provide robustness against deviations from exchangeability in the data. With no assumptions whatsoever on the underlying joint distribution of the data, it is possible to give a coverage guarantee for both existing conformal methods, and our new proposed nonexchangeable conformal procedures. The coverage gap, expressing the extent to which the guaranteed coverage level is lower than what would be guaranteed under exchangeability, is bounded by a weighted sum of total variation distances between the residual vectors obtained by swapping the iith point with the (n+1)(n+1)st point.

Our work opens the door to applying conformal prediction in applications where the data is globally likely far from exchangeable but locally deviates mildly from exchangeability. Tags and weights can be prudently used to downweight “far away” points during training and calibration, and recover reasonable coverage in practice. We hope our work will lead to more targeted methods that focus on custom design of nonsymmetric algorithms and weighting schemes to improve efficiency and robustness in specific applications, through the lens of nonexchangeable conformal prediction.

Appendix A Extension to general nonconformity scores

In this section, we extend our new nonexchangeable inference methods for split and full conformal to the setting of general nonconformity scores. The response is no longer required to be real-valued, so we will consider the general setting with data points (Xi,Yi)∈𝒳×𝒴(X_{i},Y_{i})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}.

For split conformal, as usual, we assume that the nonconformity score function S^:𝒳×𝒴→ℝ\widehat{S}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is pre-fitted. The nonexchangeable split conformal set is given by

C^n​(Xn+1)={y∈𝒴:S^​(Xn+1,y)≤𝖰1−α​(∑i=1nw~i⋅δS^​(Xi,Yi)+w~n+1⋅δ+∞)}.\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})=\left\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:\widehat{S}(X_{n+1},y)\leq\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot\delta_{\widehat{S}(X_{i},Y_{i})}+\tilde{w}_{n+1}\cdot\delta_{+\infty}\right)\right\}. (28)

For the special case S^​(x,y)=|y−μ^​(x)|\widehat{S}(x,y)=|y-\widehat{\mu}(x)| (where μ^\widehat{\mu} is a pre-fitted function), note that this reduces to the previous definition (11) from before.

For full conformal, we now consider algorithms 𝒜\mathcal{A} of the form

𝒜:∪n≥0(𝒳×𝒴×𝒯)n→{measurable functions S^:𝒳×𝒴→ℝ}.\mathcal{A}:\ \cup_{n\geq 0}\left(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{T}\right)^{n}\ \rightarrow\ \left\{\textnormal{measurable functions $\widehat{S}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$}\right\}. (29)

(As before, the symmetric algorithm setting, with no tags tit_{i}, is simply a special case of this general formulation.) First, for any y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R} and any k∈[n+1]k\in[n+1], define

S^y,k=𝒜((Xπk​(i),Yπk​(i)y,ti):i∈[n+1]),\widehat{S}^{y,k}=\mathcal{A}\left((X_{\pi_{k}(i)},Y^{y}_{\pi_{k}(i)},t_{i}):i\in[n+1]\right),

where the permutation πk\pi_{k} is defined as before (that swaps indices kk and n+1n+1), and where

Yyi=Yi,i=1,…,n,Yyn+1=y,Y^{y}_{i}=Y_{i},\ i=1,\ldots,n,\quad Y^{y}_{n+1}=y,

as before. Define the scores from this model,

Siy,k=S^y,k(Xi,Yi),i=1,…,n,Sn+1y,k=S^y,k(Xn+1,y).S^{y,k}_{i}=\widehat{S}^{y,k}(X_{i},Y_{i}),\ i=1,\dots,n,\quad S^{y,k}_{n+1}=\widehat{S}^{y,k}(X_{n+1},y).

Then, after drawing a random index KK as in (17), the prediction set is given by

C^n​(Xn+1)={y∈𝒴:Sn+1y,K≤𝖰1−α​(∑i=1n+1w~i⋅δSiy,K)}.\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})=\left\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:S^{y,K}_{n+1}\leq\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot\delta_{S^{y,K}_{i}}\right)\right\}. (30)

For the special case S^​(x,y)=|y−μ^​(x)|\widehat{S}(x,y)=|y-\widehat{\mu}(x)| (where μ^\widehat{\mu} is fitted on the same data), this again reduces to the previous definition (18) from before.

Importantly, the same theoretical result (i.e., Theorem 2) holds for these more general methods as well. The proof does not fundamentally rely on residual scores, and the modifications required for the general case are straightforward, so we omit the details here.

Appendix B Nonexchangeable jackknife+

B.1 Background

The jackknife+ [Barber et al., 2021] (closely related to “cross-conformal prediction” [Vovk, 2015]) is a method that offers a compromise between the computational and statistical costs of the split and full conformal methods. For each i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n, define the iith leave-one-out model as

μ^−i=𝒜⁡((X1,Y1),…,(Xi−1,Yi−1),(Xi+1,Yi+1),…,(Xn,Yn)),\widehat{\mu}_{-i}=\mathcal{A}\big((X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{i-1},Y_{i-1}),(X_{i+1},Y_{i+1}),\dots,(X_{n},Y_{n})\big), (31)

fitted to the training data with iith point removed. Define also the iith leave-one-out residual RiLOO=|Yi−μ^−i​(Xi)|R_{i}^{\textnormal{LOO}}=|Y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{-i}(X_{i})|, which avoids overfitting since data point (Xi,Yi)(X_{i},Y_{i}) is not used for training μ^−i\widehat{\mu}_{-i}. The jackknife+ prediction interval is then given by77 7 Abusing notation, here 𝖰α​(⋅)\mathsf{Q}_{\alpha}(\cdot) is used to denote the largest possible α\alpha-quantile if it is not unique, while as before, 𝖰1−α​(⋅)\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}(\cdot) denotes the smallest possible (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile if not unique.

[𝖰α(∑i=1n1n+1⋅δμ^−i​(Xn+1)−RiLOO+1n+1⋅δ−∞),𝖰1−α(∑i=1n1n+1⋅δμ^−i​(Xn+1)+RiLOO+1n+1⋅δ+∞)].\Bigg[\mathsf{Q}_{\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tfrac{1}{n+1}\cdot\delta_{\widehat{\mu}_{-i}(X_{n+1})-R^{\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}}+\tfrac{1}{n+1}\cdot\delta_{-\infty}\right),\\ \mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tfrac{1}{n+1}\cdot\delta_{\widehat{\mu}_{-i}(X_{n+1})+R^{\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}}+\tfrac{1}{n+1}\cdot\delta_{+\infty}\right)\Bigg]. (32)

While in practice the jackknife+ generally provides coverage close to the target level 1−α1-\alpha (and provably so under a stability assumption on 𝒜\mathcal{A}), its theoretical guarantee only ensures 1−2​α1-2\alpha probability of coverage in the worst case:

Theorem 4 (Jackknife+ [Barber et al., 2021]).

If (X1,Y1),…,(Xn,Yn),(Xn+1,Yn+1)(X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{n},Y_{n}),(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1}) are i.i.d. (or more generally, exchangeable), and the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} treats the input data points symmetrically as in (6), then the jackknife+ prediction interval defined in (32) satisfies

ℙ{Yn+1∈C^n(Xn+1)}≥1−2α.\mathbb{P}\left\{{Y_{n+1}\in\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})}\right\}\geq 1-2\alpha.

This method can be viewed as a form of nn-fold cross-validation; more generally, the CV+ method [Barber et al., 2021] uses KK-fold cross-validation for any desired KK, and obtains a similar distribution-free guarantee.

B.2 Methods

We next present the nonexchangeable jackknife+ method.

Nonexchangeable jackknife+ with a symmetric algorithm.

We first consider the setting where the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is symmetric. To begin, we choose weights wi∈[0,1]w_{i}\in[0,1], i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n, which are fixed ahead of time, and as before, this gives rise to normalized weights as in (10). The prediction interval is then given by

[𝖰α(∑i=1nw~i⋅δμ^−i​(Xn+1)−RiLOO+w~n+1⋅δ−∞),𝖰1−α(∑i=1nw~i⋅δμ^−i​(Xn+1)+RiLOO+w~n+1⋅δ+∞)],\Bigg[\mathsf{Q}_{\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot\delta_{\widehat{\mu}_{-i}(X_{n+1})-R^{\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}}+\tilde{w}_{n+1}\cdot\delta_{-\infty}\right),\\ \mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot\delta_{\widehat{\mu}_{-i}(X_{n+1})+R^{\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}}+\tilde{w}_{n+1}\cdot\delta_{+\infty}\right)\Bigg], (33)

where μ^−i\widehat{\mu}_{-i} is defined as in (31), and RiLOO=|Yi−μ^−i​(Xi)|R^{\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}=|Y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{-i}(X_{i})| as before.

Analogous to split and full conformal, here the original (unweighted) version of jackknife+ is recovered by choosing weights w1=⋯=wn=1w_{1}=\dots=w_{n}=1 in the new algorithm.

Nonexchangeable jackknife+ with a nonsymmetric algorithm.

We now extend the nonexchangeable jackknife+ to allow for a nonsymmetric algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A}. For any k∈[n+1]k\in[n+1] and any i∈[n]i\in[n], define the model μ^−ik\widehat{\mu}^{k}_{-i} as

μ^−ik=𝒜((Xπk​(j),Yπk​(j),tj):j∈[n+1],πk(j)∉{i,n+1}).\widehat{\mu}^{k}_{-i}=\mathcal{A}\left((X_{\pi_{k}(j)},Y_{\pi_{k}(j)},t_{j}):j\in[n+1],\pi_{k}(j)\not\in\{i,n+1\}\right).

As before, πk\pi_{k} is the permutation on [n+1][n+1] that swaps indices kk and n+1n+1 (or, the identity permutation in the case k=n+1k=n+1). Equivalently,

μ^k−i={𝒜((Xj,Yj,tj):j∈[n]\{i,k},(Xk,Yk,tn+1)), if ​k∈[n]​ and ​k≠i,𝒜((Xj,Yj,tj):j∈[n]\{i}), if ​k=n+1​ or ​k=i.\widehat{\mu}^{k}_{-i}=\begin{cases}\mathcal{A}\left((X_{j},Y_{j},t_{j}):j\in[n]\backslash\{i,k\},(X_{k},Y_{k},t_{n+1})\right),&\textnormal{ if }k\in[n]\textnormal{ and }k\neq i,\\ \mathcal{A}\left((X_{j},Y_{j},t_{j}):j\in[n]\backslash\{i\}\right),&\textnormal{ if }k=n+1\textnormal{ or }k=i.\end{cases}

In other words, this model is fitted on the training data (X1,Y1),…,(Xn,Yn)(X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{n},Y_{n}) but with the iith point removed, and furthermore the data point (Xk,Yk)(X_{k},Y_{k}) is given the tag tn+1t_{n+1} rather than tkt_{k}. (We note that computing the fitted model μ^−ik\widehat{\mu}^{k}_{-i} does not require knowledge of the test point (Xn+1,Yn+1)(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1}), because πk​(j)=n+1\pi_{k}(j)=n+1 is excluded from the data set when running 𝒜\mathcal{A}.) For the model μ^−ik\widehat{\mu}^{k}_{-i}, we define its corresponding leave-one-out residuals as

Rik,LOO=|Yi−μ^−ik​(Xi)|.R^{k,\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}=|Y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}^{k}_{-i}(X_{i})|.

To run the method, we first draw a random index KK as in (17), and then compute the nonexchangeable jackknife+ prediction interval as

[𝖰α(∑i=1nw~i⋅δμ^−iK​(Xn+1)−RiK,LOO+w~n+1⋅δ−∞),𝖰1−α(∑i=1nw~i⋅δμ^−iK​(Xn+1)+RiK,LOO+w~n+1⋅δ+∞)].\Bigg[\mathsf{Q}_{\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot\delta_{\widehat{\mu}^{K}_{-i}(X_{n+1})-R^{K,\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}}+\tilde{w}_{n+1}\cdot\delta_{-\infty}\right),\\ \mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot\delta_{\widehat{\mu}^{K}_{-i}(X_{n+1})+R^{K,\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}}+\tilde{w}_{n+1}\cdot\delta_{+\infty}\right)\Bigg]. (34)

Again, as was the case for nonexchangeable conformal, this method is a generalization of the symmetric case for nonexchangeable jackknife+, which was presented above.

B.3 Theory

As for the proof for nonexchangeable full conformal, we first need to define how we map a data sequence z=(z1,…,zn+1)∈(𝒳×ℝ)n+1z=(z_{1},\dots,z_{n+1})\in(\mathcal{X}\times\mathbb{R})^{n+1}, with entries zi=(xi,yi)z_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i}), to the residuals Rjack+​(z)R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(z). In the setting of jackknife+, however, the residuals are now a matrix rather than a vector. Given zz, we define (n+12){n+1\choose 2} leave-two-out models: for each i,j∈[n+1]i,j\in[n+1] with i≠ji\neq j, let

μ^−i​j=μ^−j​i=𝒜((xk,yk,tk):k∈[n+1]\{i,j}).\widehat{\mu}_{-ij}=\widehat{\mu}_{-ji}=\mathcal{A}\big((x_{k},y_{k},t_{k}):k\in[n+1]\backslash\{i,j\}\big).

Then define the matrix of residuals Rjack+​(z)∈ℝ(n+1)×(n+1)R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(z)\in\mathbb{R}^{(n+1)\times(n+1)} with entries

(Rjack+​(z))i​j=|yi−μ^−i​j​(xi)|,\big(R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(z)\big)_{ij}=|y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{-ij}(x_{i})|,

for all i≠ji\neq j, and zeros on the diagonal.

Theorem 5 (Nonexchangeable jackknife+).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an algorithm mapping a sequence of triplets (Xi,Yi,ti)(X_{i},Y_{i},t_{i}) to a fitted function as in (16). Then the nonexchangeable jackknife+ defined in (34) satisfies

ℙ{Yn+1∈C^n(Xn+1)}≥1−2α−∑i=1nw~i⋅𝖽𝖳𝖵(Rjack+(Z),Rjack+(Zi)).\mathbb{P}\left\{{Y_{n+1}\in\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})}\right\}\geq 1-2\alpha-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}\big(R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(Z),R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(Z^{i})\big).

The proof of this result is given in Appendix E.4 below. To summarize, we see that the coverage gap is bounded by

∑i=1nw~i⋅𝖽𝖳𝖵​(Rjack+​(Z),Rjack+​(Zi)).\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(Z),R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(Z^{i})).

As for the full conformal guarantee, this therefore implies the coverage gap is bounded by ∑iw~i⋅𝖽𝖳𝖵​(Z,Zi),\sum_{i}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(Z,Z^{i}), as well. Again, while this last bound can be viewed as more interpretable, in many settings it is substantially more loose.

While jackknife+ is defined specifically for the residual-based nonconformity score (i.e., the score |y−μ^​(x)||y-\widehat{\mu}(x)| to measure the extent to which a data point (x,y)(x,y) does not conform to observed trends in the data), in other settings we may wish to use alternative nonconformity scores. Jackknife+ is closely related to earlier work on the cross-conformal method [Vovk, 2015, Vovk et al., 2018]. Unlike jackknife+, the cross-conformal method can be applied to arbitrary nonconformity scores. In Appendix D, we will present a nonexchangeable version of the cross-conformal algorithm.

Appendix C Huber-robustness of conformal prediction

In this section, we consider an alternative form of robustness, which requires stricter assumptions on the distribution drift but will yield a stronger predictive coverage guarantee. First, consider a version of the classic Huber contamination model from robust statistics, where most of the data is i.i.d. from the target distribution 𝒟target\mathcal{D}_{\textnormal{target}}, but some fraction ϵ\epsilon of the data is arbitrarily corrupted. For simplicity, to start we consider observing training data point Zi=(Xi,Yi)Z_{i}=(X_{i},Y_{i}) from the mixture model

𝒟i=(1−ϵ)​𝒟target+ϵ​𝒟i′.\mathcal{D}_{i}=(1-\epsilon)\mathcal{D}_{\textnormal{target}}+\epsilon\mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{i}. (35)

Here 𝒟i′\mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{i} denotes an arbitrary adversarial distribution, that could potentially corrupt the iith training data point. However, we want to ensure coverage with respect to the target distribution 𝒟target\mathcal{D}_{\textnormal{target}}—that is, the test point Zn+1=(Xn+1,Yn+1)Z_{n+1}=(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1}) will be drawn from 𝒟target\mathcal{D}_{\textnormal{target}}. Standard conformal prediction assumes ϵ=0\epsilon=0. But, one may ask: how badly can such adversarial corruptions hurt coverage? Here, we will answer that question, but do so in a slightly more general manner. First, define a new measure of distance between distributions,

𝖽mix(𝒟,𝒟′)=inf{t≥0:𝒟=(1−t)⋅𝒟′+t⋅𝒟′′ for some distribution 𝒟′′}.\mathsf{d}_{\textnormal{mix}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})=\inf\left\{t\geq 0:\mathcal{D}=(1-t)\cdot\mathcal{D}^{\prime}+t\cdot\mathcal{D}^{\prime\prime}\textnormal{ for some distribution $\mathcal{D}^{\prime\prime}$}\right\}. (36)

Abusing notation, we will write 𝖽mix​(Z,Z′)=𝖽mix​(𝒟,𝒟′)\mathsf{d}_{\textnormal{mix}}(Z,Z^{\prime})=\mathsf{d}_{\textnormal{mix}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}^{\prime}) if Z∼𝒟Z\sim\mathcal{D} and Z′∼𝒟′Z^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}.

This “distance” can be thought of as measuring the contamination of 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime}, in the Huber sense. Indeed, if the data did indeed come from the mixture model in (35), then we would have 𝖽mix​(Zi,Zn+1)≤ϵ\mathsf{d}_{\textnormal{mix}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1})\leq\epsilon. (We note that 𝖽mix\mathsf{d}_{\textnormal{mix}} is not a metric, and in particular, is not symmetric in its two arguments.)

We now state our theory for our weighted version of split conformal, full conformal, and jackknife+, in a more restricted setting where the data points are independent and the algorithm is symmetric. From this point on we assume w1+⋯+wn>0w_{1}+\dots+w_{n}>0 to avoid a trivial setting. Define

w¯i=wiw1+⋯+wn,i=1,…,n.\bar{w}_{i}=\frac{w_{i}}{w_{1}+\dots+w_{n}},\ i=1,\dots,n.
Theorem 6 (Multiplicative bounds).

Suppose that Z1,…,Zn+1Z_{1},\dots,Z_{n+1} are independent. For any symmetric algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the nonexchangeable full conformal method (12) satisfies

ℙ{Yn+1∉C^n(Xn+1)}≤α1−∑i=1nw¯i⋅𝖽mix​(Zi,Zn+1)\mathbb{P}\left\{{Y_{n+1}\notin\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})}\right\}\leq\frac{\alpha}{1-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bar{w}_{i}\cdot\mathsf{d}_{\textnormal{mix}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1})}

(which includes the nonexchangeable split conformal method (11) as a special case), and the nonexchangeable jackknife+ method (33) satisfies

ℙ{Yn+1∉C^n(Xn+1)}≤2​α1−∑i=1nw¯i⋅𝖽mix​(Zi,Zn+1).\mathbb{P}\left\{{Y_{n+1}\notin\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})}\right\}\leq\frac{2\alpha}{1-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bar{w}_{i}\cdot\mathsf{d}_{\textnormal{mix}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1})}.

In particular, if each ZiZ_{i} follows an ϵ\epsilon-Huber contamination model relative to Zn+1Z_{n+1} as in (35), then the bound on the noncoverage rate for both unweighted and weighted conformal methods inflates by a factor of at most 1/(1−ϵ)1/(1-\epsilon), i.e., for split or full conformal prediction we get a noncoverage guarantee of α/(1−ϵ)\alpha/(1-\epsilon) instead of the nominal level α\alpha. We note that the coverage gap here is multiplicative—that is, α/(1−ϵ)≈α+α​ϵ\alpha/(1-\epsilon)\approx\alpha+\alpha\epsilon, and so the coverage gap is proportional to α\alpha. If the target error level α\alpha is small, then this multiplicative bound can offer much tighter error control, as compared to the earlier additive bounds in Theorem 2, if the terms 𝖽mix​(Zi,Zn+1)\mathsf{d}_{\textnormal{mix}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1}) are small.

On the other hand, notice that in general we have 𝖽mix​(Zi,Zn+1)≥𝖽𝖳𝖵​(Zi,Zn+1)\mathsf{d}_{\textnormal{mix}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1})\geq\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1}), and furthermore, it is possible to have 𝖽mix​(Zi,Zn+1)=1\mathsf{d}_{\textnormal{mix}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1})=1 even when 𝖽𝖳𝖵​(Zi,Zn+1)\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1}) is arbitrarily small. In a such setting the original additive bounds may give tighter results. Of course, an additional restriction is that the multiplicative bounds require independent data and symmetric algorithms, whereas the earlier theorems make no such assumptions.

Appendix D Nonexchangeable cross-conformal

While jackknife+ is defined specifically for the residual-based nonconformity score (i.e., the score |y−μ^​(x)||y-\widehat{\mu}(x)| to measure the extent to which a data point (x,y)(x,y) does not conform to observed trends in the data), in other settings we may wish to use alternative nonconformity scores. Jackknife+ is closely related to earlier work on the cross-conformal method [Vovk, 2015, Vovk et al., 2018]. Unlike jackknife+, the cross-conformal method can be applied to arbitrary nonconformity scores.

In this section, we present a nonexchangeable version of the nn-fold cross-conformal algorithm [Vovk, 2015], which can be implemented with an arbitrary nonconformity score. In the case of the regression score S^​(x,y)=|y−μ^​(x)|\widehat{S}(x,y)=|y-\widehat{\mu}(x)|, the jackknife+ prediction interval always contains the nn-fold cross-conformal prediction set. (See Barber et al. [2021] for a more detailed comparison of these methods in the exchangeable setting.)

As for the extension of nonexchangeable full conformal prediction to the setting of general nonconformity scores (in Appendix A), the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is now a function mapping tagged data sets to scoring functions, as in (29). For any k∈[n+1]k\in[n+1] and any i∈[n]i\in[n], define the iith leave-one-out scoring function S^−ik\widehat{S}^{k}_{-i} as

S^−ik=𝒜((Xπk​(i),Yπk​(i)y,ti):i∈[n+1],πk(j)∉{i,n+1}),\widehat{S}^{k}_{-i}=\mathcal{A}\left((X_{\pi_{k}(i)},Y^{y}_{\pi_{k}(i)},t_{i}):i\in[n+1],\pi_{k}(j)\not\in\{i,n+1\}\right),

or equivalently,

S^k−i={𝒜((Xj,Yj,tj):j∈[n]\{i,k},(Xk,Yk,tn+1)), if ​k∈[n]​ and ​k≠i,𝒜((Xj,Yj,tj):j∈[n]\{i}), if ​k=n+1​ or ​k=i.\widehat{S}^{k}_{-i}=\begin{cases}\mathcal{A}\Big((X_{j},Y_{j},t_{j}):j\in[n]\backslash\{i,k\},(X_{k},Y_{k},t_{n+1})\Big),&\textnormal{ if }k\in[n]\textnormal{ and }k\neq i,\\ \mathcal{A}\left((X_{j},Y_{j},t_{j}):j\in[n]\backslash\{i\}\right),&\textnormal{ if }k=n+1\textnormal{ or }k=i.\end{cases}

As before, πk\pi_{k} is the permutation on [n+1][n+1] that swaps indices kk and n+1n+1 (or, the identity permutation in the case k=n+1k=n+1). In other words, this scoring function is fitted on the training data (X1,Y1),…,(Xn,Yn)(X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{n},Y_{n}) but with the iith point removed, and furthermore the data point (Xk,Yk)(X_{k},Y_{k}) is given the tag tn+1t_{n+1} rather than tkt_{k}. We then define the corresponding leave-one-out scores as

Sik,LOO=S^−ik​(Xi,Yi).S^{k,\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}=\widehat{S}^{k}_{-i}(X_{i},Y_{i}).

Finally, to define the prediction set, we first draw a random index KK as in (17), and then compute the nonexchangeable cross-conformal prediction set as

C^n​(Xn+1)={y∈𝒴:Sn+1K,LOO≤𝖰1−α​(∑i=1n+1w~i⋅δSiK,LOO)}.\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})=\left\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:S^{K,\textnormal{LOO}}_{n+1}\leq\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot\delta_{S^{K,\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}}\right)\right\}.

As for the exchangeable setting, in the special case of the standard nonconformity score S​(x,y)=|y−μ^​(x)|S(x,y)=|y-\widehat{\mu}(x)|, the nonexchangeable nn-fold cross-conformal prediction set defined here is always contained inside the nonexchangeable jackknife+ prediction interval defined in (34).

Importantly, the same guarantee that holds for jackknife+, i.e., the result of Theorem 5, also holds for the nn-fold cross-conformal method run with an arbitrary nonconformity score. The proof of this coverage guarantee is essentially the same as for jackknife+ and so we omit it here for brevity. (For the exchangeable case, the connection between the proofs for these two different methods is explained in detail in Barber et al. [2021], and extends in a straightforward way to the nonexchangeable case considered here.)

Appendix E Additional proofs and calculations

E.1 Proof of Lemma 1

First, by the maximal coupling theorem (e.g., [Ross and Peköz, 2007, Proposition 2.7]), there exists a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} on a pair of random variables (Zi′,Zn+1′)(Z_{i}^{\prime},Z_{n+1}^{\prime}) such that, marginally, Zi′=dZiZ_{i}^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{d}}}{{=}}Z_{i} and Zn+1′=dZn+1Z_{n+1}^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{d}}}{{=}}Z_{n+1}, and such that

ℙ{Zi′=Zn+1′}=1−𝖽𝖳𝖵(Zi,Zn+1).\mathbb{P}\left\{{Z_{i}^{\prime}=Z_{n+1}^{\prime}}\right\}=1-\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1}).

Now let Z=(Z1,…,Zn+1)Z=(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{n+1}), with ZjZ_{j} drawn independently for each j∈[n+1]j\in[n+1], then draw (Zi′,Zn+1′),(Zi′′,Zn+1′′)∼iid𝒟(Z_{i}^{\prime},Z_{n+1}^{\prime}),(Z_{i}^{\prime\prime},Z_{n+1}^{\prime\prime})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{D}, independently from ZZ. Define

Z′=(Z1,…,Zi−1,Zi′,Zi+1,…,Zn,Zn+1′′),Z^{\prime}=(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{i-1},Z_{i}^{\prime},Z_{i+1},\dots,Z_{n},Z_{n+1}^{\prime\prime}),

and

Z′′=(Z1,…,Zi−1,Zi′′,Zi+1,…,Zn,Zn+1′).Z^{\prime\prime}=(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{i-1},Z_{i}^{\prime\prime},Z_{i+1},\dots,Z_{n},Z_{n+1}^{\prime}).

Then clearly, Z′=dZ′′=dZZ^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{d}}}{{=}}Z^{\prime\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{d}}}{{=}}Z. In particular, recalling the swapped indices notation (2), this implies that (Z′′)i=dZi(Z^{\prime\prime})^{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{d}}}{{=}}Z^{i}, and so

𝖽𝖳𝖵​(Z,Zi)=𝖽𝖳𝖵​(Z′,(Z′′)i).\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(Z,Z^{i})=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(Z^{\prime},(Z^{\prime\prime})^{i}).

Again applying the maximal coupling theorem, we have

𝖽𝖳𝖵​(Z′,(Z′′)i)\displaystyle\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(Z^{\prime},(Z^{\prime\prime})^{i}) ≤1−ℙ{Z′=(Z′′)i}\displaystyle\leq 1-\mathbb{P}\left\{{Z^{\prime}=(Z^{\prime\prime})^{i}}\right\}
=1−ℙ⁡{Zi′=Zn+1′,Zi′′=Zn+1′′}\displaystyle=1-\mathbb{P}\left\{{Z_{i}^{\prime}=Z_{n+1}^{\prime},Z_{i}^{\prime\prime}=Z_{n+1}^{\prime\prime}}\right\}
=1−ℙ{Zi′=Zn+1′}⋅ℙ{Zi′′=Zn+1′′}\displaystyle=1-\mathbb{P}\left\{{Z_{i}^{\prime}=Z_{n+1}^{\prime}}\right\}\cdot\mathbb{P}\left\{{Z_{i}^{\prime\prime}=Z_{n+1}^{\prime\prime}}\right\}
=1−(1−𝖽𝖳𝖵​(Zi,Zn+1))2\displaystyle=1-\left(1-\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1})\right)^{2}
=2​𝖽𝖳𝖵​(Zi,Zn+1)−𝖽𝖳𝖵​(Zi,Zn+1)2,\displaystyle=2\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1})-\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1})^{2},

completing the proof.

E.2 Proof of Theorem 3

Since nonexchangeable split conformal is simply a special case of nonexchangeable full conformal, we only need to prove the result for full conformal. We recall from the proof of Theorem 2, found in Section 6.2, that for nonexchangeable full conformal, the coverage event can be characterized as

Yn+1∈C^n​(Xn+1)⇔Rn+1Yn+1,K≤𝖰1−α​(∑i=1n+1w~i⋅δRiYn+1,K),Y_{n+1}\in\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})\ \iff\ R^{Y_{n+1},K}_{n+1}\leq\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot\delta_{R^{Y_{n+1},K}_{i}}\right),

or equivalently,

Yn+1∈C^n​(Xn+1)⇔R​(ZK)K≤𝖰1−α​(∑i=1n+1w~πK​(i)⋅δR​(ZK)i).Y_{n+1}\in\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})\ \iff\ R(Z^{K})_{K}\leq\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{\pi_{K}(i)}\cdot\delta_{R(Z^{K})_{i}}\right).

Therefore,

ℙ{Yn+1∈C^n(Xn+1)}\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left\{{Y_{n+1}\in\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})}\right\}
=ℙ{R(ZK)K≤𝖰1−α(∑i=1n+1w~πK​(i)⋅δR​(ZK)i)}\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left\{{R(Z^{K})_{K}\leq\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{\pi_{K}(i)}\cdot\delta_{R(Z^{K})_{i}}\right)}\right\}
=∑k=1n+1ℙ{K=k and R(Zk)k≤𝖰1−α(∑i=1n+1w~πk​(i)⋅δR​(Zk)i)}\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\mathbb{P}\left\{{K=k\textnormal{ and }R(Z^{k})_{k}\leq\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{\pi_{k}(i)}\cdot\delta_{R(Z^{k})_{i}}\right)}\right\}
=∑k=1n+1w~k⋅ℙ{R(Zk)k≤𝖰1−α(∑i=1n+1w~πk​(i)⋅δR​(Zk)i)}\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{k}\cdot\mathbb{P}\left\{{R(Z^{k})_{k}\leq\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{\pi_{k}(i)}\cdot\delta_{R(Z^{k})_{i}}\right)}\right\}
≤∑k=1n+1w~k⋅ℙ{R(Z)k≤𝖰1−α(∑i=1n+1w~πk​(i)⋅δR​(Z)i)}\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{k}\cdot\mathbb{P}\left\{{R(Z)_{k}\leq\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{\pi_{k}(i)}\cdot\delta_{R(Z)_{i}}\right)}\right\}
+∑k=1n+1w~k⋅𝖽𝖳𝖵(R(Z),R(Zk))\displaystyle\hskip 150.0pt+\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{k}\cdot\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(R(Z),R(Z^{k}))
=𝔼[∑k=1n+1w~k⋅𝟙{R(Z)k≤𝖰1−α(∑i=1n+1w~πk​(i)⋅δR​(Z)i)}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[{\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{k}\cdot{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{R(Z)_{k}\leq\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{\pi_{k}(i)}\cdot\delta_{R(Z)_{i}}\right)}\right\}}\right]
+∑k=1n+1w~k⋅𝖽𝖳𝖵(R(Z),R(Zk)).\displaystyle\hskip 150.0pt+\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{k}\cdot\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(R(Z),R(Z^{k})).

Here, as in the proof of Theorem 2, the third equality holds as KK is drawn independently from ZZ. Below, we will show that, for any distinct and fixed r1,…,rn+1∈ℝr_{1},\dots,r_{n+1}\in\mathbb{R}, it holds that

∑k=1n+1w~k⋅𝟙{rk≤𝖰1−α(∑i=1n+1w~πk​(i)⋅δri)}<1−α+w~n+1.\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{k}\cdot{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{k}\leq\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{\pi_{k}(i)}\cdot\delta_{r_{i}}\right)}\right\}<1-\alpha+\tilde{w}_{n+1}. (37)

Applying this inequality with ri=R​(Z)ir_{i}=R(Z)_{i} (and recalling, by assumption in the theorem, the values R​(Z)1,…,R​(Z)n+1R(Z)_{1},\dots,R(Z)_{n+1} are distinct with probability 1), we obtain

ℙ{Yn+1∈C^n(Xn+1)}≤1−α+w~n+1+∑k=1n+1w~k⋅𝖽𝖳𝖵(R(Z),R(Zk)),\mathbb{P}\left\{{Y_{n+1}\in\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})}\right\}\leq 1-\alpha+\tilde{w}_{n+1}+\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{k}\cdot\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}(R(Z),R(Z^{k})),

which would complete the proof of the theorem.

Now we need to verify (37). Define

𝒦={k∈[n+1]:rk≤𝖰1−α​(∑i=1n+1w~πk​(i)⋅δri)},\mathcal{K}=\left\{k\in[n+1]:r_{k}\leq\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{\pi_{k}(i)}\cdot\delta_{r_{i}}\right)\right\},

∑k∈𝒦w~k\displaystyle\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\tilde{w}_{k} ≤∑k=1n+1w~k⋅𝟙{rk≤rk∗}\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{k}\cdot{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{k}\leq r_{k_{*}}}\right\}
=w~k∗+∑k=1n+1w~k⋅𝟙{rk<rk∗}\displaystyle=\tilde{w}_{k_{*}}+\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{k}\cdot{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{k}<r_{k_{*}}}\right\}
=w~k∗+∑k=1n+1(w~k−w~πk∗​(k))⋅𝟙{rk<rk∗}+∑k=1n+1w~πk∗​(k)⋅𝟙{rk<rk∗}\displaystyle=\tilde{w}_{k_{*}}+\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\left(\tilde{w}_{k}-\tilde{w}_{\pi_{k_{*}}(k)}\right)\cdot{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{k}<r_{k_{*}}}\right\}+\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{\pi_{k_{*}}(k)}\cdot{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{k}<r_{k_{*}}}\right\}
<w~k∗+∑k=1n+1(w~k−w~πk∗​(k))⋅𝟙{rk<rk∗}+(1−α).\displaystyle<\tilde{w}_{k_{*}}+\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\left(\tilde{w}_{k}-\tilde{w}_{\pi_{k_{*}}(k)}\right)\cdot{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{k}<r_{k_{*}}}\right\}+(1-\alpha).

The second line holds because r1,…,rn+1r_{1},\ldots,r_{n+1} are distinct, and the last line holds by the calculations above.

If k∉{k∗,n+1}k\not\in\{k_{*},n+1\}, then πk∗​(k)=k\pi_{k_{*}}(k)=k and so the term is again zero. Therefore, we have

E.4 Proofs for the jackknife+

E.4.1 Background: proof of Theorem 4

Before proving our new results for nonexchangeable jackknife+, we first recall the proof of Theorem 4, from Barber et al. [2021], for the exchangeable case. Denote by μ^−i​j\widehat{\mu}_{-ij} the model fitted by running the symmetric algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} on the n−1n-1 data points {(Xk,Yk):k∈[n+1]\{i,j}}\big\{(X_{k},Y_{k}):k\in[n+1]\backslash\{i,j\}\big\}. Let Rjack+∈ℝ(n+1)×(n+1)R_{\textnormal{jack+}}\in\mathbb{R}^{(n+1)\times(n+1)} be the matrix with entries

(Rjack+)i​j=|Yi−μ^−i​j​(Xi)|,(R_{\textnormal{jack+}})_{ij}=|Y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{-ij}(X_{i})|,

for each i≠ji\neq j, and zeros on the diagonal. By exchangeability of the n+1n+1 data points, the matrix Rjack+R_{\textnormal{jack+}} also satisfies an exchangeability property, namely, Π⋅Rjack+⋅Π⊤=dRjack+\Pi\cdot R_{\textnormal{jack+}}\cdot\Pi^{\top}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{d}}}{{=}}R_{\textnormal{jack+}} for any fixed permutation matrix Π\Pi. Moreover, for each i∈[n]i\in[n], we have

μ^−i,(n+1)=μ^−(n+1),i=μ^−i,\widehat{\mu}_{-i,(n+1)}=\widehat{\mu}_{-(n+1),i}=\widehat{\mu}_{-i},

where μ^−i\widehat{\mu}_{-i} is the usual leave-one-out model defined earlier, and so also

(Rjack+)n+1,i=|Yn+1−μ^−i​(Xn+1)|​ and ​(Rjack+)i,n+1=RiLOO=|Yi−μ^−i​(Xi)|.(R_{\textnormal{jack+}})_{n+1,i}=|Y_{n+1}-\widehat{\mu}_{-i}(X_{n+1})|\textnormal{ and }(R_{\textnormal{jack+}})_{i,n+1}=R^{\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}=|Y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{-i}(X_{i})|.

Next, define the set of “strange” points

𝒮(Rjack+)={i∈[n+1]:∑j=1n+1𝟙{(Rjack+)i​j>(Rjack+)j​i}≥(1−α)(n+1)}.\mathcal{S}(R_{\textnormal{jack+}})=\left\{i\in[n+1]\ :\ \sum_{j=1}^{n+1}{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{(R_{\textnormal{jack+}})_{ij}>(R_{\textnormal{jack+}})_{ji}}\right\}\geq(1-\alpha)(n+1)\right\}.

In [Barber et al., 2021, Proof of Theorem 1] it is shown that the bound

|𝒮⁡(Rjack+)|≤2​α​(n+1)|\mathcal{S}(R_{\textnormal{jack+}})|\leq 2\alpha(n+1)

must hold deterministically as a consequence of Landau’s theorem for tournaments [Landau, 1953]. Furthermore, by definition of the jackknife+ prediction interval, Barber et al. [2021, Proof of Theorem 1] verify that failure of coverage, i.e., the event Yn+1∉C^n​(Xn+1)Y_{n+1}\not\in\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1}), implies that n+1∈𝒮⁡(Rjack+)n+1\in\mathcal{S}(R_{\textnormal{jack+}}). Thus, we have

ℙ{Yn+1∉C^n(Xn+1)}≤ℙ{n+1∈𝒮(Rjack+)}=1n+1∑i=1n+1ℙ{i∈𝒮(R)}≤2α,\mathbb{P}\left\{{Y_{n+1}\not\in\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})}\right\}\leq\mathbb{P}\left\{{n+1\in\mathcal{S}(R_{\textnormal{jack+}})}\right\}=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\mathbb{P}\left\{{i\in\mathcal{S}(R)}\right\}\leq 2\alpha,

where the equality holds due to the exchangeability property of the matrix Rjack+R_{\textnormal{jack+}}, while the last step follows the bound on the size of the set of “strange” points.

E.4.2 Proof of Theorem 5

Observe that, for i∈[n]i\in[n],

(Rjack+​(ZK))πK​(i),K=|Yi−μ^−iK​(Xi)|=RiK,LOO,\big(R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(Z^{K})\big)_{\pi_{K}(i),K}=|Y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}^{K}_{-i}(X_{i})|=R^{K,\textnormal{LOO}}_{i},

where πK\pi_{K} is the permutation swapping indices KK and n+1n+1 as before, and also

(Rjack+​(ZK))K,πK​(i)=|Yn+1−μ^−iK​(Xn+1)|.\big(R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(Z^{K})\big)_{K,\pi_{K}(i)}=|Y_{n+1}-\widehat{\mu}^{K}_{-i}(X_{n+1})|.

Therefore,

∑i=1nw~i⋅𝟙{|Yn+1−μ^−iK(Xn+1)|>RiK,LOO}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{|Y_{n+1}-\widehat{\mu}^{K}_{-i}(X_{n+1})|>R^{K,\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}}\right\}
=∑i=1nw~i⋅𝟙{(Rjack+(ZK))K,πK​(i)>(Rjack+(ZK))πK​(i),K}\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{\big(R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(Z^{K})\big)_{K,\pi_{K}(i)}>\big(R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(Z^{K})\big)_{\pi_{K}(i),K}}\right\}

Next, by its construction, we can verify that the noncoverage event satisfies

Yn+1∉C^n(Xn+1)⟹∑i=1nw~i⋅𝟙{|Yn+1−μ^−iK(Xn+1)|>RiK,LOO}≥1−α.Y_{n+1}\not\in\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})\ \implies\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{|Y_{n+1}-\widehat{\mu}^{K}_{-i}(X_{n+1})|>R^{K,\textnormal{LOO}}_{i}}\right\}\geq 1-\alpha.

Yn+1∉C^n(Xn+1)⟹∑i=1n+1w~i⋅𝟙{(Rjack+(ZK))K​i>(Rjack+(ZK))i​K}≥1−α.Y_{n+1}\not\in\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})\ \implies\ \sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{\big(R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(Z^{K})\big)_{Ki}>\big(R_{\textnormal{jack+}}(Z^{K})\big)_{iK}}\right\}\geq 1-\alpha. (38)

E.4.3 Proof of Lemma 2

Lemma 2 is stated and proved in Lei and Candès [2021b]; we reproduce the proof here for completeness since that paper is currently an unpublished manuscript. For each i∈𝒮i\in\mathcal{S}, by definition of 𝒮\mathcal{S}, we have

1−α≤∑j=1n+1w~j𝟙{ri​j>rj​i}≤∑j∈𝒮⁡(r)w~j𝟙{ri​j>rj​i}+∑j∈[n+1]\𝒮⁡(r)w~j=∑j∈𝒮⁡(r)w~j𝟙{ri​j>rj​i}+1−∑j∈𝒮⁡(r)w~j,1-\alpha\leq\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{j}{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{ij}>r_{ji}}\right\}\leq\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{j}{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{ij}>r_{ji}}\right\}\;+\sum_{j\in[n+1]\backslash\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{j}\\ =\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{j}{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{ij}>r_{ji}}\right\}+1-\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{j},

where the last step holds since ∑i=1n+1w~i=1\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\tilde{w}_{i}=1 by definition. Taking a weighted sum over i∈𝒮⁡(r)i\in\mathcal{S}(r),

(1−α)∑i∈𝒮⁡(r)w~i≤∑i∈𝒮⁡(r)w~i⋅[∑j∈𝒮⁡(r)w~j𝟙{ri​j>rj​i}+1−∑j∈𝒮⁡(r)w~j].(1-\alpha)\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}\leq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}\cdot\left[\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{j}{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{ij}>r_{ji}}\right\}+1-\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{j}\right].

Rearranging terms, we have

(∑i∈𝒮⁡(r)w~i)2\displaystyle\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}\right)^{2} ≤∑i,j∈𝒮⁡(r)w~iw~j𝟙{ri​j>rj​i}+α∑i∈𝒮⁡(r)w~i\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}\tilde{w}_{j}{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{ij}>r_{ji}}\right\}+\alpha\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}
=12∑i,j∈𝒮⁡(r)w~iw~j(𝟙{ri​j>rj​i}+𝟙{rj​i>ri​j})+α∑i∈𝒮⁡(r)w~i\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}\tilde{w}_{j}\left({\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{ij}>r_{ji}}\right\}+{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{r_{ji}>r_{ij}}\right\}\right)+\alpha\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}
≤12​∑i,j∈𝒮⁡(r)w~i​w~j+α​∑i∈𝒮⁡(r)w~i=12​(∑i∈𝒮⁡(r)w~i)2+α​∑i∈𝒮⁡(r)w~i.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}\tilde{w}_{j}+\alpha\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}\right)^{2}+\alpha\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}.

Rearranging terms again we have

12​(∑i∈𝒮⁡(r)w~i)2≤α⁡(∑i∈𝒮⁡(r)w~i)⟹∑i∈𝒮⁡(r)w~i≤2​α,\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}\right)^{2}\leq\alpha\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}\right)\ \implies\ \sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\tilde{w}_{i}\leq 2\alpha,

which proves the lemma.

E.5 Proof of Theorem 6

To prove the theorem, we first need a lemma on weighted sums of Bernoulli random variables. Its proof will follow shortly.

Lemma 3.

Fix p1,…,pn,a1,…,an∈[0,1]p_{1},\dots,p_{n},a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\in[0,1], with a1+⋯+an>0a_{1}+\dots+a_{n}>0. Let B1,…,BnB_{1},\dots,B_{n} be independent, with Bi∼Bernoulli​(pi)B_{i}\sim\textnormal{Bernoulli}(p_{i}). Then

a1+⋯+an+1a1​p1+⋯+an​pn+1≤𝔼⁡[a1+⋯+an+1a1​B1+⋯+an​Bn+1]≤a1+⋯+ana1​p1+⋯+an​pn.\frac{a_{1}+\dots+a_{n}+1}{a_{1}p_{1}+\dots+a_{n}p_{n}+1}\leq\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{a_{1}+\dots+a_{n}+1}{a_{1}B_{1}+\dots+a_{n}B_{n}+1}}\right]\leq\frac{a_{1}+\dots+a_{n}}{a_{1}p_{1}+\dots+a_{n}p_{n}}.

The lower bound clearly holds by Jensen’s inequality, but the upper bound is more challenging to prove. Several special cases of this upper bound are well-known in the multiple testing literature. For example, the case where a1=⋯=an=1a_{1}=\dots=a_{n}=1 and p1=⋯=pnp_{1}=\dots=p_{n} is proved in [Storey et al., 2004, Theorem 3] and used for proving FDR control of Storey’s modification of the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure [Storey, 2002]. The case where p1=⋯=pnp_{1}=\dots=p_{n} (and a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n} are arbitrary) can be found in [Ramdas et al., 2019, Lemma 3] and is used for proving FDR control for a hierarchical multiple testing procedure (the p-filter).

We are now ready to prove the theorem. By definition of 𝖽mix\mathsf{d}_{\textnormal{mix}} (36), note that we can view Z1,…,Zn+1Z_{1},\dots,Z_{n+1} as being generated by the following procedure.

  • •

    Draw C1,…,CnC_{1},\dots,C_{n} independently, with Ci∼Bernoulli​(𝖽mix​(Zi,Zn+1))C_{i}\sim\textnormal{Bernoulli}(\mathsf{d}_{\textnormal{mix}}(Z_{i},Z_{n+1})).

  • •

    For each i∈[n]i\in[n] with Ci=0C_{i}=0, and for i=n+1i=n+1, draw ZiZ_{i} i.i.d. from the distribution of Zn+1Z_{n+1}.

  • •

    For each i∈[n]i\in[n] with Ci=1C_{i}=1, draw ZiZ_{i} from the contamination distribution, i.e., the distribution 𝒟′′\mathcal{D}^{\prime\prime} achieving the infimum in (36) (applied with 𝒟\mathcal{D} and 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} equal to the distribution of ZiZ_{i} and of Zn+1Z_{n+1}, respectively).

ℙ{Yn+1∉C^n(Xn+1)|C1,…,Cn}≤α∑i=1nw~i𝟙{Ci=0}+w~n+1,\mathbb{P}\left\{{Y_{n+1}\not\in\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})}\ \middle|\ {C_{1},\dots,C_{n}}\right\}\leq\frac{\alpha}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{w}_{i}{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{C_{i}=0}\right\}+\tilde{w}_{n+1}}, (41)

while for nonexchangeable jackknife+,

ℙ{Yn+1∉C^n(Xn+1)|C1,…,Cn}≤2​α∑i=1nw~i𝟙{Ci=0}+w~n+1.\mathbb{P}\left\{{Y_{n+1}\not\in\widehat{C}_{n}(X_{n+1})}\ \middle|\ {C_{1},\dots,C_{n}}\right\}\leq\frac{2\alpha}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{w}_{i}{\mathbbm{1}}\left\{{C_{i}=0}\right\}+\tilde{w}_{n+1}}. (42)

E.5.1 Proof of Lemma 3

The lower bound holds by Jensen’s inequality. For the upper bound, we will instead prove the claim

𝔼⁡[a⊤​𝟏+c+1a⊤​B+c+1]≤a⊤​𝟏+ca⊤​p+c,\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c+1}{a^{\top}B+c+1}}\right]\leq\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c}{a^{\top}p+c}, (43)

for any c≥0c\geq 0 and any p1,…,pn,a1,…,an∈[0,1]p_{1},\dots,p_{n},a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\in[0,1] with a1+⋯+an+c>0a_{1}+\dots+a_{n}+c>0, where a=(a1,…,an)a=(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}), p=(p1,…,pn)p=(p_{1},\dots,p_{n}), B=(B1,…,Bn)B=(B_{1},\dots,B_{n}), and as before, the expectation is taken with respect to independent Bernoulli random variables Bi∼Bernoulli​(pi)B_{i}\sim\textnormal{Bernoulli}(p_{i}). Initially this appears stronger than the claim in the lemma (i.e., the lemma claims this bound only for the case c=0c=0), but in fact these claims are equivalent.

To see why, suppose that the lemma holds and now we want to prove (43) for some p,a∈[0,1]np,a\in[0,1]^{n} and some c>0c>0. Let m≥cm\geq c be any integer, and let p~,a~∈[0,1]n+m\tilde{p},\tilde{a}\in[0,1]^{n+m} be defined as

p~=(p1,…,pn,1​…,1),a~=(a1,…,an,c/m,…,c/m).\tilde{p}=(p_{1},\dots,p_{n},1\dots,1),\ \tilde{a}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{n},c/m,\dots,c/m).

Then writing B~=(B~1,…,B~n+m)\tilde{B}=(\tilde{B}_{1},\dots,\tilde{B}_{n+m}) for independent BernoullisB~i∼Bernoulli​(p~i)\tilde{B}_{i}\sim\textnormal{Bernoulli}(\tilde{p}_{i}), the claim (43) is equivalent to

𝔼⁡[a~⊤​𝟏+1a~⊤​B~+1]≤a~⊤​𝟏a~⊤​p~,\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{\tilde{a}^{\top}\mathbf{1}+1}{\tilde{a}^{\top}\tilde{B}+1}}\right]\leq\frac{\tilde{a}^{\top}\mathbf{1}}{\tilde{a}^{\top}\tilde{p}},

which holds by applying the lemma with p~,a~,n+m\tilde{p},\tilde{a},n+m in place of p,a,np,a,n.

Case 1: a1=⋯=an=1a_{1}=\dots=a_{n}=1 and p1=⋯=pnp_{1}=\dots=p_{n}.

Proving that (43) holds for this case is equivalent to proving that

𝔼⁡[n+c+1A+c+1]≤n+cn​p1+c\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{n+c+1}{A+c+1}}\right]\leq\frac{n+c}{np_{1}+c}

for A∼Binomial​(n,p1)A\sim\textnormal{Binomial}(n,p_{1}). In particular, if c=0c=0, then this is the well-known bound 𝔼⁡[n+1A+1]≤1p1\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{n+1}{A+1}}\right]\leq\frac{1}{p_{1}} (e.g., [Storey et al., 2004, Theorem 3]), while if p1=0p_{1}=0 then the result is trivial. If instead c>0c>0 and p1>0p_{1}>0, then we calculate

𝔼⁡[n+c+1A+c+1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{n+c+1}{A+c+1}}\right] =1+𝔼⁡[n−AA+c+1]\displaystyle=1+\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{n-A}{A+c+1}}\right]
=1+∑k=0n−1ℙ{A=k}⋅n−kk+c+1\displaystyle=1+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbb{P}\left\{{A=k}\right\}\cdot\frac{n-k}{k+c+1}
=1+1−p1p1⋅∑k=0n−1ℙ{A=k+1}⋅k+1k+c+1\displaystyle=1+\frac{1-p_{1}}{p_{1}}\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbb{P}\left\{{A=k+1}\right\}\cdot\frac{k+1}{k+c+1}
=1+1−p1p1⋅𝔼⁡[AA+c]\displaystyle=1+\frac{1-p_{1}}{p_{1}}\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{A}{A+c}}\right]
≤1+1−p1p1⋅𝔼⁡[A]𝔼⁡[A]+c=n+cn​p1+c,\displaystyle\leq 1+\frac{1-p_{1}}{p_{1}}\cdot\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[{A}\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[{A}\right]+c}=\frac{n+c}{np_{1}+c},

where the inequality holds by Jensen’s inequality.

Case 2: a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n} arbitrary and p1=⋯=pnp_{1}=\dots=p_{n}.

Proving that (43) holds for this next case is equivalent to proving that

𝔼⁡[a⊤​𝟏+c+1a⊤​B+c+1]≤a⊤​𝟏+ca⊤​𝟏⋅p1+c.\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c+1}{a^{\top}B+c+1}}\right]\leq\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c}{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}\cdot p_{1}+c}.

For the special case c=0c=0, this result is shown in [Ramdas et al., 2019, Lemma 3]. Let A=(A1,…,An)A=(A_{1},\dots,A_{n}), where Ai∼Bernoulli​(ai)A_{i}\sim\textnormal{Bernoulli}(a_{i}) are drawn independently for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, and A⟂⁣⟂BA\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 2.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 2.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 2.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 2.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}B. Note that, conditional on BB, it holds that A⊤​B⟂⁣⟂A⊤​(𝟏−B)A^{\top}B\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 2.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 2.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 2.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 2.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}A^{\top}(\mathbf{1}-B). Therefore,

𝔼⁡[A⊤​𝟏+c+1A⊤​B+c+1|B]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{A^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c+1}{A^{\top}B+c+1}}\ \middle|\ {B}\right] =1+𝔼⁡[A⊤​(𝟏−B)A⊤​B+c+1|B]\displaystyle=1+\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{A^{\top}(\mathbf{1}-B)}{A^{\top}B+c+1}}\ \middle|\ {B}\right]
=1+𝔼⁡[A⊤​(𝟏−B)|B]⋅𝔼⁡[1A⊤​B+c+1|B]\displaystyle=1+\mathbb{E}\left[{A^{\top}(\mathbf{1}-B)}\ \middle|\ {B}\right]\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{1}{A^{\top}B+c+1}}\ \middle|\ {B}\right]
≥1+𝔼⁡[A⊤​(𝟏−B)|B]𝔼⁡[A⊤​B+c+1|B]​ (by Jensen’s inequality)\displaystyle\geq 1+\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[{A^{\top}(\mathbf{1}-B)}\ \middle|\ {B}\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[{A^{\top}B+c+1}\ \middle|\ {B}\right]}\textnormal{ (by Jensen's inequality)}
=1+a⊤​(𝟏−B)a⊤​B+c+1=a⊤​𝟏+c+1a⊤​B+c+1,\displaystyle=1+\frac{a^{\top}(\mathbf{1}-B)}{a^{\top}B+c+1}=\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c+1}{a^{\top}B+c+1},

and therefore after marginalizing over BB, we obtain

Next, writing S=A⊤​𝟏S=A^{\top}\mathbf{1}, we see that A⊤​BA^{\top}B follows a Binomial(S,p1)(S,p_{1}) distribution conditional on SS, and therefore,

𝔼⁡[A⊤​𝟏+c+1A⊤​B+c+1|S]=𝔼⁡[S+c+1Binomial​(S,p1)+c+1|S]≤S+cS​p1+c,\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{A^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c+1}{A^{\top}B+c+1}}\ \middle|\ {S}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{S+c+1}{\textnormal{Binomial}(S,p_{1})+c+1}}\ \middle|\ {S}\right]\leq\frac{S+c}{Sp_{1}+c},

where the last step holds by case 1. We can also observe that s↦s+cs​p1+cs\mapsto\frac{s+c}{sp_{1}+c} is a concave function, and so

Case 3: a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n} and p1,…,pnp_{1},\ldots,p_{n} arbitrary.

In this final case, we will prove (43), proceeding by induction on nn. For n=1n=1, this reduces to case 1, so we can proceed to the case n≥2n\geq 2. Without loss of generality, assume p1≤⋯≤pnp_{1}\leq\dots\leq p_{n}. If pn=0p_{n}=0 then the claim is trivial. Otherwise, let Ai∼Bernoulli​(pi/pn)A_{i}\sim\textnormal{Bernoulli}(p_{i}/p_{n}) for i=1,…,n−1i=1,\dots,n-1, and let Ci∼Bernoulli​(pn)C_{i}\sim\textnormal{Bernoulli}(p_{n}) for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n, with A1,…,An−1,C1,…,CnA_{1},\dots,A_{n-1},C_{1},\dots,C_{n} all drawn independently. Then a1​B1+⋯+an​Bn=da1​A1​C1+⋯+an−1​An−1​Cn−1+an​Cna_{1}B_{1}+\dots+a_{n}B_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{d}}}{{=}}a_{1}A_{1}C_{1}+\dots+a_{n-1}A_{n-1}C_{n-1}+a_{n}C_{n}.

Next, define random weights W=(W1,…,Wn)W=(W_{1},\dots,W_{n}), where Wi=ai​AiW_{i}=a_{i}A_{i} for each i=1,…,n−1i=1,\dots,n-1 and Wn=anW_{n}=a_{n}. Then by case 2, we have

𝔼⁡[W1+⋯+Wn+c+1W1​C1+⋯+Wn​Cn+c+1|W]≤W⊤​𝟏+cW⊤​𝟏⋅pn+c.\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{W_{1}+\dots+W_{n}+c+1}{W_{1}C_{1}+\dots+W_{n}C_{n}+c+1}}\ \middle|\ {W}\right]\leq\frac{W^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c}{W^{\top}\mathbf{1}\cdot p_{n}+c}.

𝔼⁡[a−n⊤​A+an+c+1a⊤​B+c+1|A]≤a−n⊤​A+an+c(a−n⊤​A+an)⋅pn+c=1pn−c⁡(1pn−1)(a−n⊤​A+an)⋅pn+c.\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{a_{-n}^{\top}A+a_{n}+c+1}{a^{\top}B+c+1}}\ \middle|\ {A}\right]\leq\frac{a_{-n}^{\top}A+a_{n}+c}{(a_{-n}^{\top}A+a_{n})\cdot p_{n}+c}=\frac{1}{p_{n}}-\frac{c\left(\frac{1}{p_{n}}-1\right)}{(a_{-n}^{\top}A+a_{n})\cdot p_{n}+c}.

Thus,

𝔼⁡[a⊤​𝟏+c+1a⊤​B+c+1]=𝔼⁡[a⊤​𝟏+c+1a−n⊤​A+an+c+1⋅a−n⊤​A+an+c+1a⊤​B+c+1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c+1}{a^{\top}B+c+1}}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c+1}{a_{-n}^{\top}A+a_{n}+c+1}\cdot\frac{a_{-n}^{\top}A+a_{n}+c+1}{a^{\top}B+c+1}}\right]
=𝔼⁡[a⊤​𝟏+c+1a−n⊤​A+an+c+1⋅𝔼⁡[a−n⊤​A+an+c+1a⊤​B+c+1|A]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c+1}{a_{-n}^{\top}A+a_{n}+c+1}\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{a_{-n}^{\top}A+a_{n}+c+1}{a^{\top}B+c+1}}\ \middle|\ {A}\right]}\right]
≤𝔼⁡[a⊤​𝟏+c+1a−n⊤​A+an+c+1⋅(1pn−c⁡(1pn−1)(a−n⊤​A+an)⋅pn+c)]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c+1}{a_{-n}^{\top}A+a_{n}+c+1}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{p_{n}}-\frac{c\left(\frac{1}{p_{n}}-1\right)}{(a_{-n}^{\top}A+a_{n})\cdot p_{n}+c}\right)}\right]
≤𝔼⁡[a⊤​𝟏+c+1a−n⊤​A+an+c+1]⋅𝔼⁡[1pn−c⁡(1pn−1)(a−n⊤​A+an)⋅pn+c],\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c+1}{a_{-n}^{\top}A+a_{n}+c+1}}\right]\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{1}{p_{n}}-\frac{c\left(\frac{1}{p_{n}}-1\right)}{(a_{-n}^{\top}A+a_{n})\cdot p_{n}+c}}\right], (44)

where the last step holds since the first quantity is a monotone decreasing function of a−n⊤​Aa_{-n}^{\top}A, and the second quantity is a monotone increasing function of a−n⊤​Aa_{-n}^{\top}A. By induction, we can apply (43) at size n−1n-1 in place of nn to see that the first expected value is bounded as

Moreover, applying Jensen’s inequality, we calculate

Combining these calculations with (44) above, we have

𝔼⁡[a⊤​𝟏+c+1a⊤​B+c+1]≤pn⋅a⊤​𝟏+ca⊤​p+c​pn⋅a⊤​p+c​pnpn​(a⊤​p+c)=a⊤​𝟏+ca⊤​p+c,\mathbb{E}\left[{\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c+1}{a^{\top}B+c+1}}\right]\leq p_{n}\cdot\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c}{a^{\top}p+cp_{n}}\cdot\frac{a^{\top}p+cp_{n}}{p_{n}(a^{\top}p+c)}=\frac{a^{\top}\mathbf{1}+c}{a^{\top}p+c},

which proves that (43) holds as desired.

Appendix F Simulations for split conformal and jackknife+

The simulations presented in Section 5.1 used only full conformal methods. In this section, we repeat these simulated data experiments with split conformal prediction and jackknife+. The same data is used in these experiments as was generated for the results in Section 5.1. (Code for reproducing these additional experiments is available at https://rinafb.github.io/code/nonexchangeable_conformal.zip.)

For split conformal prediction, we split the training data indices [n][n] by assigning odd indices to the training set and even indices to the holdout set. The methods compared for split conformal are SplitCP+LS, NexSplitCP+LS, NexSplitCP+WLS, defined exactly as the full conformal experiments but with split conformal in place of full conformal. For jackknife+, the methods compare are Jack+LS, NexJack+LS, NexJack+WLS, again defined analogously.

For both split conformal and jackknife+, the details for defining μ^\widehat{\mu} for choosing the weights wiw_{i} and tags tit_{i} are exactly the same as for the full conformal experiments given in Section 5.1. Also as in the full conformal experiments, after a burn-in period of the first 100 time points, at each time n=100,…,N−1n=100,\dots,N-1 we run the inference methods with training data i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n and test point n+1n+1. The results shown are averaged over 200 independent replications of the simulation.

Results for split conformal and for jackknife+ are summarized in Tables 5 and 5, respectively, while Figures 5 and 6 display the average coverage and the prediction interval width over the time range of the simulation. Overall, we see similar trends as for the full conformal prediction experiments in Section 5.1, where for the i.i.d. data in Setting 1 the performance of all three versions of each method are comparable, while for the changepoint data in Setting 2 and the distribution drift data in Setting 3, the original methods lose coverage substantially, while nonexchangeable versions of split conformal and of jackknife+ remain closer to the target coverage level, and the nonsymmetric algorithm (weighted least squares) allows for a narrower prediction interval.

Appendix G Election data set description

To prepare the data, we followed the protocol from Gibbs and Candès [2021] and, therefore, quote from the above reference:

The county-level demographic characteristics used for prediction were the proportion of the total population that fell into each of the following race categories (either alone or in combination): black or African American, American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Native Hawaiian or other Pacific islander. In addition to this, we also used the proportion of the total population that was male, of Hispanic origin and that fell within each of the age ranges 20-29, 30-44, 45-64, and 65+. Demographic information was obtained from 2019 estimates published by the United States Census Bureau and available at [United States Census Bureau, 2019a]. In addition to these demographic features we also used the median household income and the percentage of individuals with a bachelors degree or higher as covariates. Data on county-level median household incomes was based on 2019 estimates obtained from [United States Census Bureau, 2019c]. The percentage of individuals with a bachelors degree or higher was computed based on data collected during the years 2015-2019 and published at [United States Census Bureau, 2019b]. As an aside, we remark that we used 2019 estimates because this was the most recent year for which data was available.

For 2016 covariate data, we used the same data sources, subject to the important distinction that we—almost exclusively—used published figures available by 2016. (The U.S. Census Bureau sometimes updates its figures so we cannot rule out the possibility that a few entries were changed post 2016.) Finally, vote counts for the 2016 election were obtained from MIT Election Data and Science Lab [2018], while 2020 election data was taken from Leip [2020]. In total, matching covariate and election vote count data were obtained for 3111 counties. Merging 2016 and 2020 data left us with 3076 counties (1119 in the training set and 1957 in the test set).
